# Reattempt A | Version 6 | Solutions

*Each question earns **Pass** or **Not Yet**. Pass (high) and Pass (low) mark the range of passing work; both earn the same Pass.*

## Q1 | Opportunity Cost (A1.1)

Suppose Honeydukes, a candy shop in Hogsmeade, can make $12$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs *or* $9$ pounds of Ice Mice in one day.

::: solution

**What to look for:**

**Pass (high):** Both per-unit tradeoffs and the best alternative forgone for each choice.

**Pass (low):** Correct ratios with an arithmetic slip, or an omitted unit made clear by the work.

**Not Yet:** Reversed tradeoffs, adding all alternatives, or missing evidence of the best alternative.

:::

a\) What is Honeydukes’ opportunity cost of $1$ pound of Ice Mice? **4/3 pounds of Chocolate Frogs**

::: solution

a\) **4/3 pounds of Chocolate Frogs**: giving up 12 pounds of Chocolate Frogs buys 9 pounds of Ice Mice, so one pound of Ice Mice costs $12/9 = 4/3$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs.

:::

b\) What is Honeydukes’ opportunity cost of $1$ pound of Chocolate Frogs? **3/4 pound of Ice Mice**

::: solution

b\) **3/4 pound of Ice Mice**, the reciprocal.

:::

c\) Honeydukes ranks its options for the day from best (1) to worst (3):

> 1. Cater a Hogwarts feast (C)
> 2. Sell candy in the shop (S)
> 3. Restock the cellar (R)

 (i) What is Honeydukes’ opportunity cost of choosing S? **Catering a Hogwarts feast (C)**

::: solution

c\) (i) C, its best alternative to S.

:::

 (ii) What is Honeydukes’ opportunity cost of choosing C? **Selling candy in the shop (S)**

::: solution

c\) (ii) S, its next best option after C.

:::

# Reattempt A | Version 6 | Solutions

## Q2 | Absolute and Comparative Advantage (A2.1)

Honeydukes and Zonkos are two candy shops in Hogsmeade, the only all-wizarding village in Britain. In one day, Honeydukes can make $12$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs or $9$ pounds of Ice Mice, and Zonkos can make $30$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs or $6$ pounds of Ice Mice. Set up a Production Table with both shops’ output per day. Then set up an Opportunity Cost table with both shops’ opportunity costs for each good. Which shop has the absolute advantage (AA) and comparative advantage (CA) in each good?

::: solution

**What to look for:**

**Pass (high):** Production and cost tables; AA from greater output and CA from lower opportunity cost.

**Pass (low):** A copying or arithmetic slip and its consistent consequences when the method and comparisons are clear.

**Not Yet:** Using output to choose CA, systematically reversing costs, or wrong answers with no cost work to show where the error came from. Correct answers earned Pass even without the cost work shown.

:::

:::: solution

**Production table:** each shop’s output per day if it makes only that good, straight from the setup.

::: {.table style=grid}

|   |   |   |
| --- | --- | --- |
|   | **Chocolate Frogs** | **Ice Mice** |
| **Honeydukes** | 12 pounds | 9 pounds |
| **Zonkos** | 30 pounds | 6 pounds |

:::

**Opportunity costs:** each cell is what the shop gives up of the other good. Honeydukes: a pound of Chocolate Frogs costs $9/12 = 3/4$ pound of Ice Mice, a pound of Ice Mice costs $12/9 = 4/3$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs. Zonkos: a pound of Chocolate Frogs costs $6/30 = 1/5$ pound of Ice Mice, a pound of Ice Mice costs $30/6 = 5$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs.

::: {.table style=grid}

|   |   |   |
| --- | --- | --- |
|   | **Chocolate Frogs** | **Ice Mice** |
| **Honeydukes** | 3/4 Ice Mice | 4/3 Chocolate Frogs |
| **Zonkos** | 1/5 Ice Mice | 5 Chocolate Frogs |

:::

::::

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

AA in Chocolate Frogs: **Zonkos**

:::

::: column

CA in Chocolate Frogs: **Zonkos**

:::

::::

:::: {.columns .continued gutter=1em}

::: column

AA in Ice Mice: **Honeydukes**

:::

::: column

CA in Ice Mice: **Honeydukes**

:::

::::

::: solution

AA in Chocolate Frogs: **Zonkos** ($30 > 12$). AA in Ice Mice: **Honeydukes** ($9 > 6$).

CA in Chocolate Frogs: **Zonkos** ($1/5 < 3/4$). CA in Ice Mice: **Honeydukes** ($4/3 < 5$). Here each shop holds both advantages in the same good.

:::

# Reattempt A | Version 6 | Solutions

## Q3 | Zonkos’ PPF (A1.2)

Suppose Zonkos, a candy shop in Hogsmeade, can make $30$ pounds of Chocolate Frogs ($F$) *or* $6$ pounds of Ice Mice ($M$) in one day. There are two graphs, one beside (a) and one beside (b). On both graphs, draw Zonkos’ PPF, $F$ on the vertical axis and $M$ on the horizontal. Label the intercepts.

::: solution

**What to look for:**

**Pass (high):** A meaningful PPF, inside/on/outside classifications, and the effect of each capacity change.

**Pass (low):** An isolated wrong or missing label when the graph and other answers establish the distinction.

**Not Yet:** No usable PPF graph, repeated category confusion, or a wrong capacity-change answer without supporting evidence.

:::

a\) For each daily output, write whether it is unattainable, inefficient, or efficient, and mark it on the first graph.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=62.264%}

(i\) $15F$ and $3M$ **Efficient**

(ii\) $29F$ **Inefficient**

(iii\) $30F$ **Efficient**

(iv\) $30F$ and $1M$ **Unattainable**

:::

::: {.column width=37.736%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

:::

::::

::: solution

**PPF:** Straight line from $30F$ to $6M$, so $F = 30 - 5M$. Opportunity cost: $5F$ per $M$. **a) In order:** Efficient ($30 - 5 \cdot 3 = 15$); Inefficient (just inside the vertical intercept); Efficient (the vertical intercept); Unattainable (above the frontier).

:::

b\) Zonkos currently makes $20F$ and $2M$. On the second graph, draw its PPF and mark this output. Is that output unattainable, inefficient, or efficient:

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=62.264%}

(i\) if investors at Gringotts lay off many of Zonkos’ employees? **Unattainable**

(ii\) if instead it buys a more capable Ice Mice machine, doubling its daily output of Ice Mice? **Inefficient**

:::

::: {.column width=37.736%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

:::

::::

::: solution

**b)** The original bundle is on the original frontier ($30 - 5 \cdot 2 = 20$). (i) Layoffs: both intercepts fall and the frontier shifts in; **unattainable**. (ii) Machine: the $M$ intercept doubles to $12$, $F$ stays at $30$; at $2M$ the new frontier allows $25F$, so the original bundle is **inefficient**. **Taylor’s Note:** In Q3.b, new frontiers illustrate the shifts but they are not required in the answer.

:::

# Reattempt A | Version 6 | Solutions

## Q4 | Specialization and Trade (A3.1)

Honeydukes and Zonkos each make Jelly Slugs and Sugar Quills. Their opportunity costs are listed in the following opportunity cost table.

::: {.table style=grid}

|   |   |   |
| --- | --- | --- |
|   | **Jelly Slug** | **Sugar Quill** |
| **Zonkos** | 4 Sugar Quills | 1/4 Jelly Slug |
| **Honeydukes** | 5/4 Sugar Quills | 4/5 Jelly Slug |

:::

::: solution

**What to look for:**

**Endpoints:** The bounds identify an open interval. At an endpoint one producer is indifferent.

**Pass (high):** The lower-cost specializer, the full trade interval in common units, and an acceptable rate.

**Pass (low):** Correct specializer, bounds, and acceptable selection plus one extra outside checkbox.

**Not Yet:** Wrong specialization or bounds without correct work, only outside rates selected, or multiple extra selections.

:::

a\) If the two shops specialize and trade with each other, which one should specialize in Sugar Quills? **Zonkos**

::: solution

a\) **Zonkos**, the shop with the lower opportunity cost of a Sugar Quill. Honeydukes has the lower cost of a Jelly Slug (5/4 versus 4 Sugar Quills) and Zonkos the lower cost of a Sugar Quill (1/4 versus 4/5 Jelly Slug).

:::

b\) What is the range of exchange rates that would make both Honeydukes and Zonkos better off?

Between **5/4** and **4** Sugar Quills for $1$ Jelly Slug

::: solution

b\) Between **5/4** and **4** Sugar Quills for $1$ Jelly Slug: the two shops’ opportunity costs of a Jelly Slug, read down the Jelly Slug column. Below the low end the Jelly Slug maker would rather keep its Jelly Slugs; above the high end the Sugar Quill maker would rather make Jelly Slugs itself.

:::

c\) Select all the exchange rates which could facilitate a trade between the two shops.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

☐ 1 Jelly Slug for 5 Sugar Quills

:::

::: column

☒ 1 Jelly Slug for 3 Sugar Quills

:::

::::

:::: {.columns .continued gutter=1em}

::: column

☒ 1 Jelly Slug for 2 Sugar Quills

:::

::: column

☐ 1 Jelly Slug for 1 Sugar Quill

:::

::::

::: solution

c\) **1 Jelly Slug for 3 Sugar Quills** and **1 Jelly Slug for 2 Sugar Quills**. 1 is below Honeydukes’ cost of 5/4, so Honeydukes keeps its Jelly Slugs; 5 is above Zonkos’ cost of 4, so Zonkos would rather make Jelly Slugs itself.

:::
